client: I've been trying to get back into hiking with my friends like I used to before the breakup, but it just feels empty now. I keep catching myself looking at the trails Maria and I used to walk together, and then the whole outing just feels pointless. Part of me thinks talking about this won't change anything - those memories are just going to keep haunting me no matter what.
therapist:
I hear both resignation and pain in your voice as you talk about these hiking trips—it sounds like the memories with Maria are casting a shadow over something that used to bring you joy. When you say talking won’t change anything, I wonder if that thought itself is making the emptiness feel heavier than it needs to be.  

Would you be open to exploring how those memories affect you *now* versus how they might shift over time? The way your voice quickens tells me this still feels very raw, and that’s okay.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It's not even about whether the memories will fade—I *know* they will. But right now everything just feels... contaminated, I guess? Like even if I force myself to keep hiking, those trails will always be "the places we went together" first, and "places I enjoy" second. I hate that she gets to ruin this for me.
therapist:
Your voice tightens when you say "contaminated"—that word really carries the weight of how violated and resentful you feel about these places being changed for you. It’s understandable to resent that loss of something that was purely yours, and that anger has its own validity right now.  

What if we looked at this differently: could those trails become places where you reclaim parts of yourself *outside* of that relationship, rather than just reminders of what’s gone? I hear the hurt, but also a thread of determination underneath.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I see what you're saying about reclaiming the trails, but it feels like empty positive thinking. When I'm actually out there, all I can think is "Maria loved this view" or "We had that stupid argument near this log." It's like my brain won't let me have a single new memory there without dragging the old ones along.
therapist:
I hear the frustration in your voice rising as you describe this—it’s not just sadness, but almost a rebellion against how stubbornly those old memories cling. That sense of intrusion makes it hard to trust any "positive thinking" right now, and that’s completely valid.  

When you say your brain *won’t let you* have new memories there, I wonder if we could slow that thought down: are those old memories *erasing* the new ones, or just crowding them out for now? The way your voice sharpens tells me this isn’t abstract—it’s happening in real time, and that’s exhausting. Let’s honor that.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess they’re not erasing the new memories, but they definitely overpower them. Even when I’m laughing with my friends, there’s this little voice in the back of my head saying, “Remember when Maria laughed like that?” It’s exhausting, like I can’t fully enjoy anything without her ghost showing up. I don’t know how to quiet that voice—it feels like it’s just part of me now.
therapist:
There’s a weariness in how you describe this—like even laughter feels shadowed, and that little voice has worn its way into your sense of self. The way your words rush tells me how frustrating it is to feel hijacked by these reminders when you’re trying to just *be* in the moment.  

But I notice something important: you called it a *little* voice, not an all-consuming one. That distinction matters—it suggests part of you recognizes these thoughts don’t have to define every experience, even if they’re persistent right now. Would you be willing to explore how much space they actually take up versus how much space they *feel* like they take?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Huh, I never thought about the fact that I called it a "little" voice—that's actually kind of interesting. But in the moment, it *feels* all-consuming, you know? Like even if it's technically just a whisper, it's this constant static in the background that drains the color out of everything. I'm not sure measuring its exact "space" would help when the impact feels so heavy.
therapist:
I hear a shift in your voice as you catch that detail about the "little" voice—there's almost a spark of curiosity breaking through the exhaustion, even if the weight still feels overwhelming. That static analogy is so vivid; it makes sense that something constant, even quiet, could drain so much energy over time.  

Let’s hold both truths here: the voice *feels* all-consuming in the moment, *and* you just noticed something new about how you describe it. That small observation might be more important than it seems—it’s proof your mind isn’t completely hostage to this pattern, even when it’s loud.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... noticing that detail felt like a fluke, not some breakthrough. It's like when you accidentally drop something and catch it—it doesn't mean you have good reflexes, just that you got lucky once. The static is still there, and most days it feels like I'm just white-knuckling through it until I can go home and collapse.
therapist:
Your voice jumps higher as you say this—there’s real frustration in how that moment of noticing gets dismissed as just luck, like it doesn’t count unless it’s a total transformation. I hear how exhausting it is to feel like you’re constantly bracing against that static, just waiting for relief.  

But even "white-knuckling" means you’re *doing* the hard thing—that’s not nothing. What if we treated that caught moment less like a fluke and more like a clue? The way your words sped up tells me this pain is visceral, but so was that flicker of awareness. Let’s work with both.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I can see what you mean about it being a clue, but it's hard to hold onto that when the bad days still feel so much bigger than the small moments. Like, even if I notice that "little voice" thing again, it doesn't stop the ache in my chest when I see our favorite picnic spot. I don't know how to make those clues actually matter when the pain is so physical.
therapist:
I hear how thin your patience feels right now—your voice sounds frayed, almost fragile, as you talk about the physical ache outweighing those small observations. When pain sits that heavily in your body, it makes sense that mental "clues" would feel flimsy in comparison.  

But the fact that you’re still engaging with this at all—even skeptically—tells me part of you hasn’t fully surrendered to the static. What if we focused less on *stopping* the ache and more on how to breathe through it when it comes? The way your voice tightens tells me those picnic spots still feel like gut-punches, and they might for a while—but gut-punches don’t last forever.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about breathing through it, but in those moments it feels impossible to even remember to breathe. My whole body just locks up like I've been hit—how am I supposed to focus on breathing when my brain's screaming at me to run away? It's not like the ache is some quiet background thing I can gently observe.
therapist:
Your voice shakes as you describe this—it’s not just emotional pain, but a full-body panic that leaves no room for breathing techniques or gentle observation. I hear how betrayed your body feels in those moments, like it’s working against you instead of with you.  

When the brain screams to run, that’s survival instinct—not something to "fix," but something to acknowledge with fierce compassion. Would it help to name what’s happening in those locked-up moments? Not to change it yet, just to say: *This is the shock hitting, and it will pass.* I hear how fast and thin your words get when describing this—that’s the body keeping score. Let’s honor that.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Naming it does help a little, but in the moment it still feels like trying to shout over a hurricane—like my rational thoughts are so fragile compared to the physical reaction. Sometimes I worry if I acknowledge the panic too much, I'll just give it more power to overwhelm me.
therapist:
Your voice gets quieter as you say this—almost like you're holding your breath between words—and I hear that tension between wanting to manage the panic and fearing it might swallow you whole. That hurricane analogy is so vivid; it makes sense that rational thoughts would feel flimsy when your body’s reacting like it’s facing a storm.  

But here’s what stands out: you *are* still speaking, even softly. That tells me part of you knows the hurricane isn’t the whole truth, even when it feels all-consuming. What if we practiced acknowledging the panic *without* letting it define the entire moment? Not to shout over it, but to whisper alongside it until the winds die down.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: Whispering alongside it... that feels possible, I guess. But sometimes I worry that even whispering will make the panic louder, like I'm feeding it by giving it any attention at all. It's hard to trust that acknowledging it won't just make things worse.
therapist:
Your voice tightens and rises when you talk about feeding the panic—I hear how scary it feels to even *consider* engaging with it, like any attention might make it grow. That fear makes so much sense when the panic already feels so volatile and hungry.  

But notice how your words slow when you say "whispering alongside it feels possible"—there’s a quiet opening there. What if we treated the panic less like something to starve or feed, and more like weather passing through? Even whispers can remind you: *This isn’t all of me, just a storm I’m learning to walk with.*
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
